name: The World of AI: Nonprofits and Open Source Foundations catalogue page
title: The World of AI: Nonprofits and Open Source Foundations catalogue page
answer: The World of AI publishes this catalogue page of four individually verified nonprofits and open source foundations, each with a sourced classification note. Its most useful point is that the list is deliberately narrow: LMSYS stewards Chatbot Arena for open model evaluation, Khan Academy is an AI end-user in education, and the Krita and Blender foundations steward creative tools that AI imagery and 3D content intersect with. The page also states what it excludes, including training compute providers, standards bodies and open-model foundations that release weights.

sections.body: The World of AI publishes this page as part of its AI ecosystem section. It is a catalogue of four individually verified organisations under the heading Nonprofits and Open Source Foundations, each with a sourced classification note. The page says every entry carries the source that decided it and the date that source was last read. It gives a citation line with a retrieval date of 2026-09-28. No publication date is stated. The page also includes site-wide search text, promotional notes for books by Stephen R. Jordan and SRJ Consulting services, and a description of the site as an atlas of AI law, lawsuits and terms.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The page lists four organisations: two nonprofits and two open-source foundations with roles that touch AI tooling and evaluation. It says none are infrastructure builders in the compute-or-power sense. LMSYS is described as the most directly AI-central entry because it stewards Chatbot Arena, a shared evaluation platform the broader AI community uses to benchmark model quality. The page argues this neutral, open evaluation infrastructure matters because model comparison depends on it, yet it sits outside the commercial incentives of the labs being evaluated. Khan Academy is described as an end-user of AI capability in education, not a producer of it. The Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation steward creative software tools that AI-generated imagery and 3D content increasingly intersect with, but their primary missions predate and are not defined by AI. The page says classifications are made one at a time against a document the organisation published about itself, with the document recorded. It says nothing was assigned by keyword, by a model, or by inheritance from a parent company, because a classification that keeps no evidence cannot be audited and a wrong one survives quietly. It also states what the data does not cover: no training compute providers, no standards bodies setting grid or data-center specifications, and no open-model foundations that release weights for public use.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The page gives one number: four individually verified organisations, described as two nonprofits and two open-source foundations. It names LMSYS, Khan Academy, Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation. It defines LMSYS as steward of Chatbot Arena, a shared evaluation platform. It states that none are infrastructure builders in the compute-or-power sense. It says the notes confirm only organizational structure and nonprofit status, not funding scale, compute access, or governance detail. It gives a retrieval date of 2026-09-28.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in nonprofits can use this page as a small, sourced starting point for organisations that sit between AI capability and public benefit. It identifies LMSYS as open evaluation infrastructure, Khan Academy as an education end-user, and Krita and Blender as creative tool foundations touched by AI content. It also warns that the nonprofit AI infrastructure layer is not represented here, so the page is better for seeing classification method and named examples than for understanding funding, compute access or governance. Its value is the evidence trail: each entry carries a source and a last-read date.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Nonprofits

sections.body: The page is partial by its own account. It has only four entries and says the notes confirm only organizational structure and nonprofit status, not funding scale, compute access or governance detail. It excludes training compute providers, standards bodies setting grid or data-center specifications, and open-model foundations that release weights. It gives no publication date, only a retrieval date of 2026-09-28. The surrounding text includes promotional material for books by Stephen R. Jordan and SRJ Consulting services, so the page sits within a commercial site. It is a catalogue entry, not a research report.
